title: Transform derivatives before naming fields
question: How do the field equations change coordinates?
recap: In the moving observer’s coordinates the derivatives in time and along x mix. Grouping the result so that the Maxwell-Hertz equations keep their form points to the moving observer’s electric and magnetic components; the form alone does not prove that identification, which rests on the principle of relativity.
premises: The coordinates transform by the Lorentz map, and the fields obey Maxwell’s equations in empty space.
The example is in SI units, so factors of c appear explicitly.
limitations: Einstein’s Gaussian equations become SI ones by a change of units, not by renaming symbols.
A common factor on all the new fields is fixed by a separate argument, going there and back and the symmetry of space; rearranging the equations does not fix it.

overview.text: In the moving observer’s coordinates the derivatives in time and along \(x\) mix. Grouping the result so that the Maxwell-Hertz equations keep their form points to the moving observer’s electric and magnetic components; the form alone does not prove that identification, which rests on the principle of relativity.

full.spoken: Partial by partial t equals gamma times, partial by partial t prime minus v partial by partial x prime. Partial by partial x equals gamma times, partial by partial x prime minus v over c squared partial by partial t prime.

full.text: Take the simplest case, a wave travelling along \(x\) with an electric component \(E_y\) and a magnetic component \(B_z\). In SI units and empty space the Maxwell-Hertz equations reduce to the pair \(\partial_t E_y = -c^2\,\partial_x B_z\) and \(\partial_t B_z = -\partial_x E_y\). Substitute the two derivative rules above into both equations; the next step needs the pair.

After the substitution, \(E_y\) and \(B_z\) appear only in the combinations \(E_y - vB_z\) and \(B_z - vE_y/c^2\). Multiply each by \(\gamma\) and call the results \(E'_y\) and \(B'_z\). The pair then reads \(\partial_{t'} E'_y = -c^2\,\partial_{x'} B'_z\) and \(\partial_{t'} B'_z = -\partial_{x'} E'_y\), the same form as before. The field-equations laboratory shows this grouping one term at a time.

The form alone would also allow every new field to carry one common factor that depends on \(v\), and the paper keeps such a factor at first. Transforming there and back must return the original fields, so the factor’s value at \(v\) times its value at \(-v\) must be 1. By symmetry the factor cannot depend on the direction of motion, so it is the same at \(v\) and \(-v\), and the positive root makes it 1.

full.returnCaption: Return to how the field equations look in the moving frame.

steps.text: Letters: the paper writes the electric force as (X, Y, Z) and the magnetic force as (L, M, N), in Gaussian units, with V for the speed of light and β for the modern γ; in k they are \(X'\) to \(N'\). This explanation works in SI units, where the electric field is E, the magnetic field B, and a factor \(c^2\) appears that Gaussian units hide. The primed coordinates \(x'\) and \(t'\) are the paper's ξ and τ.

items: The paper begins with the Maxwell–Hertz equations for empty space, valid in K. One of them, in its letters, is \(\frac{1}{V}\frac{\partial X}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial N}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial M}{\partial z}\), and there are six in all.
To write them in k's coordinates, every derivative must be rewritten, since \(t'\) and \(x'\) each depend on both t and x: \(t'=\gamma(t-vx/c^2)\) and \(x'=\gamma(x-vt)\).

The chain rule: a change in t changes \(t'\) by γ and \(x'\) by −γv, so \(\partial_t=\gamma\partial_{t'}-\gamma v\partial_{x'}\). A change in x changes \(t'\) by \(-\gamma v/c^2\) and \(x'\) by γ, so \(\partial_x=\gamma\partial_{x'}-\gamma(v/c^2)\partial_{t'}\). Those are the two rules below.

steps.spoken: Partial by partial t equals gamma times, partial by partial t prime minus v partial by partial x prime. Partial by partial x equals gamma times, partial by partial x prime minus v over c squared partial by partial t prime.

items: Take the simplest case, a wave along x with an electric component \(E_y\) and a magnetic component \(B_z\). In SI units and empty space the equations reduce to the pair \(\partial_tE_y=-c^2\partial_xB_z\) and \(\partial_tB_z=-\partial_xE_y\).

Substitute into the first: \(\gamma(\partial_{t'}-v\partial_{x'})E_y=-c^2\gamma(\partial_{x'}-v\partial_{t'}/c^2)B_z\). Cancel γ and move the \(\partial_{t'}\) terms to the left and the \(\partial_{x'}\) terms to the right: \(\partial_{t'}(E_y-vB_z)=-c^2\partial_{x'}(B_z-vE_y/c^2)\).
Substitute into the second: \(\gamma(\partial_{t'}-v\partial_{x'})B_z=-\gamma(\partial_{x'}-v\partial_{t'}/c^2)E_y\). Collect the same way: \(\partial_{t'}(B_z-vE_y/c^2)=-\partial_{x'}(E_y-vB_z)\).

The fields now appear only in two combinations. Multiply both by γ and name them: \(E'_y=\gamma(E_y-vB_z)\) and \(B'_z=\gamma(B_z-vE_y/c^2)\). The pair becomes \(\partial_{t'}E'_y=-c^2\partial_{x'}B'_z\) and \(\partial_{t'}B'_z=-\partial_{x'}E'_y\), the same form as in K.

The paper does the same with all six equations and finds the combinations \(\beta(N-(v/V)Y)\) and \(\beta(M+(v/V)Z)\) in place of N and M. The principle of relativity requires that the Maxwell–Hertz equations hold in k too, for the forces the moving system defines by their pushes on electric and magnetic charges.
So the paper sets each new force equal to the matching combination times one common factor ψ(v), which may depend on v but not on the coordinates. The form of the equations cannot fix that factor.

Fixing it: transforming to k and back must give the original fields, so the factor's values at v and at −v multiply to 1. By symmetry, reversing v reverses the sign of a component such as \(Y'\) without changing its size, so the factor is the same at v and −v; the positive root makes it 1 (p. 909).
Worked: a wave running along +x has \(E_y=cB_z\) in SI. In a frame moving the same way at 0.6c, \(E'_y=\gamma(E_y-vB_z)=1.25\,E_y(1-0.6)=0.5\,E_y\): the field halves, as the frequency will in §7.

Keep two claims apart. That the equations keep their form after the substitution is algebra. That the new combinations are the fields the moving observer measures is the principle of relativity, applied to forces on charges at rest in k.
Changing from the paper's Gaussian units to SI is a change of units, done term by term, not a renaming of letters.

steps.returnCaption: Return to how the field equations look in the moving frame.

margin.text: Einstein writes the electric force as \(X, Y, Z\) and the magnetic force as \(L, M, N\), in Gaussian units, with \(V\) for the speed of light; his \(\beta\) is the modern \(\gamma\), not \(v/c\). The field tensor that packs all six components together came later, with Minkowski in 1908. Where this edition uses it, it checks results; it is never a step in the 1905 argument.
